Q: Can type bounds/constraints be stored in global variables and later used in generic function definitions with Python 3.14+? A:

First, you are right to point out that these signatures are not equivalent. The first uses a union, and says the result will either be bool, int, str or float, but makes no promisees about which type it will actually be. The second can be understand to mean that the result will be of the type specified by expected. For instance, if expected is str, then the result will be an instance of str.

By "understood to mean", I mean that whilst the statement is valid python syntax, it is not a valid type annotation. Most (all?) type checkers will reject it (at the very least, both mypy and pyright reject it). This is because a tuple of types is not a valid type itself. There is no way to make it a valid type, and still be able to use it the way you want to. The way you have used SCALAR_TYPES makes it look like you want to reuse the definition of a type variable. However, the new-stype type annotations that you are using, introduced by PEP 695, keep type variables isolated from one function to another. This makes it easier to keep each function isolated and allows reuse of variable names that would otherwise all have to exist in the global scope (eg. T1, T2, ... Tn). However, this makes it harder to keep type annotations DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

Alternatives

If you do want functions to be able to share the same definition of a type variable, there are at least two ways you can do this. The first is to use the old-school TypeVar, and second is to use a class as a context for your functions. For example:

TypeVar

from typing import TypeVar, reveal_type

T = TypeVar('T', int, str)

def double(x: T) -> T:
    return x * 2

# The T of `add` shares the same definition as the T of `double`
def add(x: T, y: T) -> T:
    return x + y

reveal_type(add(0, 0))  # note: Revealed type is: "int" (per mypy output)

Mypy playground link

Class context

class Namespace[T: (int, str)]:
    @staticmethod
    def double(x: T) -> T:
        return x * 2

    # The T of `add` shares the same definition as the T of `double`
    @staticmethod
    def add(x: T, y: T) -> T:
        return x + y

reveal_type(Namespace.double(0))  # note: Revealed type is "int"

# You can move the functions into the module namespace, and type checkers will still
# understand the functions and their type annotations.

double = Namespace.double
reveal_type(double(''))  # note: Revealed type is "str"

Q: Nested IF in Excel using Today() A:

This requires VBA as far as i know. With this code you can enter a name in any cell in column B (one name at a time) and todays date is added in column A in the same row. The VBA code enters only the date in column A (not a formula that returns todays date) and therefore the date in column A doesn't change.

Private Sub Worksheet_Change(ByVal Target As Excel.Range)
    If Target.Column = 2 Then
        If Target <> "" Then
            Target.Offset(0, -1).Value = Date
        Else
        End If
    End If
End Sub

Q: C++ convert vector element to string A:

example is a std::string and therefore example[index] is a single character.

But list is a vector of strings (not single characters), and so list.push_back here requires a std::string to be add to the vector.

It is not clear why you need to add a single character, but if you indeed want to do it, you can explicitly create a std::string from it:

list.push_back(std::string{ example[index] });

Q: How can I copy a WordPress/WooCommerce site from hosting to a local environment? A:

The simplest and safest way (especially if you're new to hosting panels) is to avoid manual export/import and use a backup plugin like UpdraftPlus.

Recommended Approach (Using UpdraftPlus)

  1. Install Updraft on the live site

    • Go to Plugins → Add New → Install & Activate UpdraftPlus

    • Take a full backup (Database + Plugins + Themes + Uploads + Others)

  2. Download backup files

    • Download all generated backup files:

      • Database

      • Plugins

      • Themes

      • Uploads

      • Others

  3. Set up a local WordPress environment
    You can use any of these depending on your preference:

    • Local by Flywheel (easiest for beginners)

    • XAMPP

    • WampServer

  4. Install a fresh WordPress locally

    • Create a new site using one of the above tools

  5. Install UpdraftPlus on the local site

    • Same plugin → install & activate

  6. Upload backup files locally

    • Go to:
      wp-content/updraft/

    • Paste all downloaded backup .zip files into this folder

  7. Restore the backup

    • In UpdraftPlus → “Rescan local folder”

    • Your backup will appear

    • Click Restore and select all components

  8. Handle URL changes

    • During restore, enable the option to search & replace URLs

    • This updates your live domain to your local URL automatically

Why this method is better

  • No need to manually export/import via phpMyAdmin

  • No need to edit wp-config.php or handle DB credentials

  • Automatically handles serialized data (common issue in migrations)

  • Much safer for beginners

Alternative (Manual Way)

Your understanding is correct for manual migration:

  • Files → via File Manager or FTP

  • Database → via phpMyAdmin export/import

  • Config → wp-config.php

But this approach is more error-prone (especially with URL replacement and serialized data), so using UpdraftPlus is generally faster and more reliable.
